Title: She's Softball's First $1 Million Pitcher—and She Could Be the Last; NiJaree Canady's transfer from Stanford landed her a seven-figure payday and has Texas Tech in an NCAA softball super regional. But lucrative deals like hers could soon be doomed.
Text: The Texas Tech softball team is just two wins away from the Women's College World Series for one spectacular reason.It has a pitcher worth $1 million.That's not hyperbole. Texas Tech's booster collective actually paid NiJaree Canady a cool million to transfer from Stanford, where she was already a star, and suit up for the Red Raiders this season.And it looks like money well spent. Canady is responsible for 58% of Texas Tech's wins. She has posted 28 wins against just five losses and struck out 272 batters over 191 innings pitched through Tuesday."She's one of the top women athletes, so in my mind she deserved what some of those male athletes are getting," said Tracy Sellers, who funded an endorsement from the school's donor collective with her husband, John, a former Red Raiders defensive lineman. "I hope it's setting the stage for the next girl."But athletes like Canady are suddenly an endangered species. That's because a new set of rules that would severely restrict how much boosters can pay college athletes is likely to be enacted in the coming days. The ripple effect could mean fewer softball players, golfers, sprinters and other athletes from lower-profile sports earning big paydays.If and when Judge Claudia Wilken approves a settlement to a consolidation of three antitrust lawsuits brought by athletes against the major conferences and the NCAA, two big shifts are set to take place. First, each college athletic department will be allowed to share about $20 million of its annual revenues with athletes. But roughly 90% of that money is expected to go to the marquee sports of football and men's basketball—leaving scraps for sports like softball.Second, outside deals for athletes to profit from their name, image or likeness (NIL) would begin to go through a new clearinghouse built with help from Deloitte and overseen by a new entity set up to enforce the rules enacted by the settlement.In that clearinghouse, deals by major companies like Nike or State Farm are likely to pass muster, said someone familiar with a committee set up by the Power 5 conferences and NCAA to implement the settlement. Deals like Canady's, funded primarily by booster collectives, are not."Booster deals are going to be more difficult to pass," the person familiar said, adding: "The system is set up to not allow third parties to pay for play."After Canady's sophomore season at Stanford last year, the pitcher entered the transfer portal, where a handful of powerhouse schools lined up to woo her. But it was the last place she visited—Lubbock, Texas—that won Canady over.The key piece of her move was an endorsement deal from the donor collective known as the Matador Club, worth just over $1 million.Since the Sellers became billionaires by flipping oil and gas leases in West Texas's Permian Basin, they've donated handsomely to their alma mater. The couple gave $11 million to Texas Tech athletics in 2022, including $1 million for softball facility upgrades.Canady had six-figure offers from other schools, but nothing close to what the Matador Club offered. But John Sellers, who described himself as a "ready, fire, aim" kind of guy, wanted to make a statement.But donors like the Sellers could soon become much less influential. That is down to college sports' continued resistance to characterizing athletes as employees, a move that would require a slew of new rights and regulations."I think if people/donors want to invest in sports, specifically Olympic and female sports, they should be given that opportunity," Canady said. "Oftentimes athletes in these sports don't really have opportunities to make life-changing deals after college."The NIL clearinghouse won't preclude athletes like Canady from signing endorsement deals, but it will bring considerably more oversight. The organization will want to know, for instance, how a booster club can get $1 million of value in marketing from a player with a profile like Canady, who has 34,000 followers on Instagram but is hardly a household name.Colleges' pot of revenue-sharing money won't be subject to such scrutiny, meanwhile, as long as schools stay under the $20.5 million limit. So an offensive lineman, anonymous as he may be, could receive $1 million directly from his school. But a star lacrosse player would be hard-pressed to gain approval for a $1 million outside of an NIL deal bankrolled by a wealthy alum.Some in college sports say nixing such deals risks pushing booster money back under the table—where it was for decades.For the moment, before the settlement is approved, athletes and booster collectives are scrambling to cut deals under the old regulations. The Matador Club has already signed Canady to a one-year extension worth another $1 million, according to a person familiar with the deal."Until we figure out exactly what they're going to let go on," Tracy Sellers said, "why not keep going?"Write to Rachel Bachman at Rachel.Bachman@wsj.com and Laine Higgins at laine.higgins@wsj.comBy Rachel Bachman and Laine Higgins
event_description: New rules restricting booster payments to college athletes are likely to be enacted.
setting: college sports regulatory environment
characters: NiJaree Canady [Victim]; new rules restricting booster payments [Villain]; Tracy Sellers and John Sellers [Hero]
plot: Tracy and John Sellers fund a $1 million endorsement deal for NiJaree Canady to transfer to Texas Tech, but new rules are likely to restrict booster payments, threatening the financial opportunities for athletes like Canady.
moral: The new rules threaten the financial support for athletes in lower-profile sports like softball, and Congress should ensure that athletes have the opportunity to earn fair compensation through endorsements.

Title: U.S. News: Cases Teed Up for a Split Court
Text: WASHINGTON -- An eight-member Supreme Court, divided by ideology and clouded by uncertainty, returns Monday for a docket of workmanlike disputes while senators battle over nominee Brett Kavanaugh's confirmation in the face of sexual-assault allegations. The court's calendar features cases on endangered species and excessive fines, as well as litigation over sex-offender registration that could have broad constitutional ramifications. There is also an improbable appearance for an Alaska moose hunter who is making his second trip to the court. Senate Republicans had intended to confirm Judge Kavanaugh in time to provide a fifth conservative vote by the start of the term; on the cases it hears before it has an ideological majority, the court may take only modest steps if there are divisions. Given the politics surrounding the court, it is also possible the justices will seek to cool the temperature even once its membership is full -- at least at the outset. "It's a little bit of a fraught period for the court" and the "very divided country" it serves, Justice Elena Kagan said during a Sept. 12 appearance in New York. "We should be aware of the environment and not unnecessarily exacerbate the divisions that unfortunately exist." That may be made easier by the relatively low profile of cases now pending. Nothing currently on tap promises to match the drama of the court's last term, in which the justices upheld President Trump's travel ban, weakened public-sector unions, allowed sports gambling and set new privacy protections on cellphone data. The court also tiptoed near major rulings on gay rights and partisan gerrymandering of voting maps, only to put them off for another day. Yet hot-button cases are poised to return soon. In coming months the court may decide whether to consider the Trump administration's cancellation of the DACA program that provides a temporary reprieve for illegal immigrants brought to the U.S. as children, as well as its ban on transgender military service. It may also weigh workplace protections for gay employees, the constitutionality of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and a new crop of gerrymandering cases. The passions behind such disputes help explain the bitterness and force of the current fight over who will serve on the court. The latest twist came Friday, when Sen. Jeff Flake (R., Ariz.) effectively forced a one-week delay in Judge Kavanaugh's confirmation vote so the Federal Bureau of Investigation can look into allegations of sexual misconduct when he was in high school and college. Judge Kavanaugh has repeatedly denied the allegations. The first case up Monday pits environmentalists against property-rights advocates in a dispute over how far the Endangered Species Act can go in protecting habitats. The Fish and Wildlife Service in 2012 designated protected land for the dusky gopher frog, but landowners including Weyerhaeuser Co. objected because the government included a tract where the frogs don't currently live. On Tuesday, the court will hear the first of several significant criminal-law cases when it weighs whether Congress delegated too much discretion to the executive branch in establishing a sex-offender registry. The challenger, Herman Gundy, committed a sex offense in Maryland before the federal registration law was passed in 2006. After serving time, Mr. Gundy moved to New York but didn't register, arguing he wasn't required to. Prosecutors disagreed and charged him. Mr. Gundy argues that under the separation of powers, Congress can't give the Justice Department complete discretion to decide whether to apply the law retroactively. Later in the term, the court will consider whether the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on excessive fines applies to state governments. At issue is a defendant who engaged in two small-dollar drug transactions with undercover police officers. The Indiana Supreme Court upheld the civil forfeiture of his $42,000 Land Rover, overturning a lower court that found the penalty grossly disproportionate to the offense. In another major case, the court will review a Prohibition-era precedent that allows the federal government and states to try a person for the same offense despite the constitutional prohibition on double jeopardy. The case involves a 2015 incident in which police found a handgun in an Alabama man's car. He objected to being prosecuted under federal and state laws, which both prohibit him from owning the gun because of a previous felony conviction. Separately, the court is building out its business docket, including nuts-and-bolts cases on taxes, patents and copyrights. The justices also are slated to hear an appeal by Apple Inc., which is disputing a consumer lawsuit alleging it illegally monopolized the sale of iPhone apps. Then there's the moose hunter. John Sturgeon is challenging National Park Service rules banning his hovercraft from waterways in the Yukon-Charley National Preserve, which he travels through to reach his preferred hunting grounds. He contends that Alaska state law, which would permit his hovercraft, should govern. After losing in the lower courts, Mr. Sturgeon got his case to the Supreme Court in 2016, which sent it back for further reconsideration. Lower courts again ruled for the park service, prompting this second appeal. --- Kennedy's Absence Shifts the Terrain The Supreme Court has been at the center of a political cauldron since Justice Anthony Kennedy retired. He usually was the deciding vote in the court's 5-to-4 cases. Though generally conservative, Justice Kennedy joined liberals in several high-profile areas, including expansion of gay rights and limitations on capital punishment. Attorneys appearing before the court often crafted their arguments with him in mind. "Justice Kennedy was, of course, the focus of much of the briefing and argument in recent years," U.S. Solicitor General Noel Francisco said recently. Now lawyers and the justices will face a considerable adjustment. If the justices split 4-4, they could set it for re-argument later once a ninth arrives. If the vacancy persists and a shorthanded court can't break a tie, the lower-court ruling in the case would stand.   Credit: By Brent Kendall and Jess Bravin
event_description: The Supreme Court is set to hear a case involving a dispute over the Endangered Species Act's protections for the dusky gopher frog's habitat.
setting: Supreme Court case regarding the Endangered Species Act
characters: environmentalists [Hero]; property-rights advocates [Villain]; dusky gopher frog [Victim]
plot: The Supreme Court is set to hear a case where environmentalists are advocating for the protection of the dusky gopher frog's habitat under the Endangered Species Act, while property-rights advocates, including landowners like Weyerhaeuser Co., are challenging the government's designation of protected land that includes areas where the frogs do not currently live.
moral: The court should uphold the Endangered Species Act's protections for the dusky gopher frog's habitat, as the environmentalists are fighting to preserve the species and its environment against the harmful actions of property-rights advocates.

Title: Missing Submersible Titan Planned to Sample Titanic Site for Environmental DNA; Scientists planned to look for marine life growing on the wreck using new sampling technique
Text: OceanGate's Titan voyage was planned as a mix of tourism and something else: Science. A unique ecosystem has grown around the wreck of the Titanic at the bottom of the Atlantic. The company was collaborating with researchers to sample and study that complex marine life, even as it ferried customers to view the scene . Using a relatively new technique known as environmental DNA , or eDNA, the submersible's pilot planned to collect water samples around the wreck to later analyze tiny bits of floating genetic material left behind by organisms, according to emails from OceanGate. Scientists have used this noninvasive technique for the past decade as a powerful tool to identify biodiversity in nature without bringing back parts of animal or tissue samples to the lab. It is being used by researchers around the world to track endangered species, as well as to look for powerful compounds produced by marine organisms that might have medicinal properties. "The Titanic wreck has created an oasis of biodiversity in an area of the ocean which is typically pretty barren," said Steve Barrett, chief executive officer of the genomic technology firm eDNAtec, who confirmed that the firm is working with OceanGate. "It has become an artificial reef, actually." Scientists on the surface ship that supports the submersible were planning to examine bacteria associated with the rust-colored growths on the wreck as well as animals living in the nearby bottom muds, according to an April 24 email from Lisa Dreher, an OceanGate spokeswoman. "We are trying to answer the question of how long the Titanic will look like the Titanic," Dreher said in the email. Dreher also cited Titanic archaeology and deep-ocean technology as areas of interest for an excursion that was primarily a vehicle for tourism. The firm eDNAtec has been analyzing water samples taken during OceanGate's 2022 Titanic expedition, according to Barrett. Barrett said the company built a water sampling device and attached it to the outside of the Titan submersible that could be operated by the pilot inside. The goal of the project was to observe changes in the marine life living around the wreck over time. Barrett said the plan was to collect and store the water samples taken by the submersible from the wreck site aboard the support ship, and then use genetic fingerprinting tools to identify eDNA back at the firm's lab in Canada. He said academic scientists along with eDNAtec researchers have submitted their findings from last year and are awaiting publication in a scientific journal. In addition to sampling at the Titanic site, eDNAtec is training Canadian indigenous groups to identify ecological changes in their marine environment, checking aquaculture farms for bacterial pathogens, and sampling areas for the Canadian government and energy firms to determine changes in aquatic life that might be the result of nearby mining, Barrett said. An OceanGate spokesman declined to comment. The five-person sub lost contact with its support vessel, the Polar Prince, on Sunday. Coast Guard officials Tuesday said they were continuing an aerial and ship-based search for the sub in an area 900 miles east of Massachusetts in the North Atlantic. A Canadian search plane reported hearing underwater noises that might be from the missing submersible. Those conducting the search relocated remote-operated vehicles to explore the origin of the noises but didn't find anything, the U.S. Coast Guard said in a tweet early Wednesday. "Those ROV searches have yielded negative results but continue," the Coast Guard added. Write to Eric Niiler at eric.niiler@wsj.com  Credit: By Eric Niiler
event_description: The use of environmental DNA (eDNA) to track endangered species and assess biodiversity in marine environments.
setting: a scientific expedition involving tourism and research at the Titanic wreck site in the North Atlantic
characters: OceanGate [Hero]; U.S. Coast Guard [Hero]; Titan submersible [Victim]
plot: OceanGate planned a scientific expedition to study marine life around the Titanic wreck while providing a tourism experience. The Titan submersible was used to collect water samples for eDNA analysis, but it lost contact with its support vessel, prompting a search by the U.S. Coast Guard.
moral: The search for the Titan submersible is critical to ensure the safety of those on board, and continued support for innovative research methods like eDNA sampling is essential for understanding and preserving marine biodiversity.

Title: Nearly Two-Dozen Endangered Species Are Now Extinct, U.S. Agency Says; The 23 species include plants, birds and fish, according to the Fish and Wildlife Service
Text: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service said 23 species–ranging from fish to birds–are now extinct. As a result, the federal agency is proposing delisting them from the Endangered Species Act. "For the species proposed for delisting today, the protections of the ESA [Endangered Species Act] came too late, with most either extinct, functionally extinct, or in steep decline at the timing of Listing," the Fish and Wildlife Service said Wednesday. The service said it determined the species were extinct based on reviews of the best available science. The agency stops trying to find the species and stops funding their recovery when they are removed from the ESA, said spokesman Brian Hires. It is the biggest batch of species the government has announced as extinct, said Tierra Curry, senior scientist at the Center for Biological Diversity, a nonprofit that works to prevent species from going extinct. "It's really sad because it basically means that they think the situation for these species is hopeless," she said, noting the biggest issue for the species was habitat loss through either dam construction or logging. Ms. Curry said one takeaway from the government's announcement is that endangered species need to be listed once they are in trouble, instead of waiting for them to decline so much that recovery becomes harder and more expensive. She said it takes about 12 years for a species to get on the endangered species list. Martha Williams, principal deputy director of the Fish and Wildlife Service, said the agency is actively engaged in preventing further extinctions. The Endangered Species Act has prevented more than 99% of the species listed from becoming extinct, the agency said. The Fish and Wildlife Service is seeking commentary, data and information from the public until Dec. 29 about its proposal to delist the species. Here is a look at a few on the agency's list: Ivory-Billed Woodpecker The ivory-billed woodpecker was last seen in 1944 in Louisiana and was listed as endangered in 1967. One of America's largest woodpeckers, the bird has black and white feathers on its body and red feathers on the top of its head. The Fish and Wildlife Service said the loss of mature forest habitat and collection were the main threats leading to its extinction. Freshwater Mussels The Fish and Wildlife Service determined the flat pigtoe, southern acornshell, stirrupshell, upland combshell, green-blossom pearly, turgid-blossom pearly mussel, yellow-blossom pearly mussel and tubercled-blossom pearly mussels are all extinct. Many of these mussels were last seen in the 1960s, '70s and '80s and were often found in the Southeast U.S. Bachman's Warbler The Bachman's warbler, at one time found in Florida and South Carolina, was listed as endangered in 1967. The last confirmed sighting of the small black and yellow bird was in 1988. San Marcos Gambusia The San Marcos gambusia, which earlier could be found in Texas, was last seen in 1983. The small fish, which is about one-inch long, was listed as endangered three years before that. Little Mariana Fruit Bat The Little Mariana fruit bat used to be found in Guam and was listed as endangered in 1984. The last confirmed sighting of the bat, which is less than 10 inches long and can weigh less than 1 pound , was in 1968. Another species from Guam listed by the Fish and Wildlife Service as extinct is the bridled white-eye bird, which was listed as endangered in 1984 and last seen the year prior. Hawaiian Birds The yellow Kauai akialoa bird, which has a long, curved beak that points downward, was last seen in 1969. It was listed as endangered two years before that. Other birds from Hawaii listed as extinct are the Kauai nukupuu, the Kauaʻi ʻōʻō, the large Kauai thrush, the Maui ākepa, the Maui nukupuʻu, the Molokai creeper and the po`ouli. The plant known as phyllostegia glabra var. lanaiensis was also listed as extinct. Hawaii and the Pacific islands are home to more than 650 animal and plant species that are listed as endangered, according to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Write to Allison Prang at allison.prang@wsj.com   Nearly Two-Dozen Endangered Species Are Now Extinct, U.S. Agency Says  Credit: By Allison Prang
event_description: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service is proposing to delist 23 species from the Endangered Species Act due to their extinction.
setting: federal agency rulemaking
characters: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service [Villain]; Tierra Curry [Hero]; endangered species [Victim]
plot: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service proposes to delist 23 species from the Endangered Species Act after determining they are extinct, which results in the cessation of recovery efforts and funding for these species. Tierra Curry highlights that the protections came too late, leading to their extinction due to habitat loss.
moral: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service must act more swiftly to list endangered species before they reach critical decline, as timely intervention is essential to prevent further extinctions.

Title: An Uncertain Fate for Plum Island; Developers are anxious to build on the mostly undeveloped island, but environmental groups have filed a lawsuit to prevent the sale
Text: PLUM ISLAND, N.Y.--This windswept island about the size of Central Park has the makings of a vacation destination, complete with views of Long Island Sound, and all of it a short ferry ride from Connecticut and New York. But the future of Plum Island, home to an animal disease laboratory run by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, is as murky as the fog that regularly envelopes the spit of land off the tip of Long Island's North Fork. The U.S. Congress passed legislation in 2008 directing the government to sell the island if the Department of Homeland Security found another location for the lab--which it did, eventually, in Manhattan, Kan. The lab is set to move there by 2023. Even years ahead of the move, real-estate developers have dreams of selling exclusive, waterfront homes along the island's pristine, soft-sand beaches. They are buoyed by a federal environmental report released in 2013 that found up to 500 residential homes could be built on the 840-acre island. "Plum Island is maybe one of the most important pieces of real estate to be offered on the East Coast in decades," said David Kapell, former mayor of Greenport, N.Y. on Long Island, and a real-estate broker. Environmental conservationists, however, want to see the island preserved. The island's sale is on hold due to a lawsuit filed in federal court by environmental groups. A spokesman with the Department of Homeland Security declined to comment on the suit. Most of Plum Island hasn't been developed, making it a sanctuary for wildlife. Piping plovers, listed as endangered in New York state, nest on some of its beaches, and harbor seals sun themselves on its rocky southeastern shore. In addition to the laboratory and ferry terminal, an array of empty buildings remain from the island's military past. The federal government built a coastal defense station called Fort Terry on the island for the Spanish-American War. Today, the remains of gun batteries overlook a sandy beach with aquamarine waters. The U.S. Department of Agriculture took possession of the island in 1954 to build the Plum Island Animal Disease Center. It was an optimal location to study foot-and-mouth disease, in part because the surrounding waters provided a natural defense barrier. Off limits without permission, Plum Island also has provided fodder for conspiracy theorists. One popular theory claimed that a disfigured animal that washed ashore on Montauk, dubbed the Montauk monster, was an animal experiment from the island. But officials at the lab, which has about 400 employees, dispute the claim they have something to hide. "We are secure, but we are not secret," said Larry Barrett, director of the Plum Island Animal Disease Center. "Everything we do here is published." Some of the center's current research focuses on improving vaccines for foot-and-mouth disease and for classical swine fever, said Luis Rodriguez, the USDA's research leader for the foreign animal disease research unit at Plum Island. In July, environmental groups, led by Save the Sound, sued the federal General Services Administration and the homeland security department. The suit asks the court to stop the government from selling the island at an auction. The plaintiffs said the sale would "threaten the continued existence of the endangered species that inhabit Plum Island, the ecology of the Long Island Sound." The plaintiffs said the government failed to adequately consider any reasonable alternatives that would restrict development on the island to protect its natural resources. Homeland Security says any change in its current plans would require Congress to pass a new law directing the agency to do that. All four U.S. Senators from Connecticut and New York have introduced a bill to block the sale, but it hasn't come up for a vote. Mr. Kapell said the federal government should consider selling the island to the highest bidder, but add requirements so that it doesn't get turned into a resort or a high-end residential project. He cites Robins Island, in the Peconic Bay, as an example. Hedge-fund manager Louis Bacon bought the island in 1993 and maintains a private residence there and has preserved much of the island. Plum Island is subject to some jurisdiction of the nearby Town of Southold. In 2013, Southold passed zoning that would prohibit any potential buyer from building homes or hotels there. Permitted uses include a research facility, a nature preserve and museums. "The bidder is going to have factor in the town's zoning," said Scott Russell, town supervisor of Southold. "Development of the island above and beyond what its current use is, isn't realistic." Write to Joseph De Avila at  joseph.deavila@wsj.com Related Coverage * Opponents Seek to Stop Government From Selling Plum Island * NY Lawmakers Examine Possible Uses for Plum Island * Long Island Town Lays Strategy to Protect Plum Island Credit: By Joseph De Avila
event_description: Environmental groups filed a lawsuit to stop the government from selling Plum Island.
setting: federal court case regarding the sale of Plum Island
characters: environmental groups [Hero]; U.S. Department of Homeland Security [Villain]; endangered species [Victim]
plot: Environmental groups filed a lawsuit to stop the government from selling Plum Island, arguing that the sale would threaten the endangered species inhabiting the island and that the government failed to consider alternatives to protect its natural resources.
moral: The government must halt the sale of Plum Island to protect endangered species and the ecology of Long Island Sound, ensuring that any development respects the island's natural resources.

Title: For Jobs, We Need to Encourage Young Entrepreneurs
Text: One major impediment to starting a business today is government ("Endangered Species: The Young Entrepreneur," page one, Jan. 3). The regulations, fees and taxes, even if you don't make a profit or have a payroll, can be insurmountable. For example, take the Affordable Care Act. Ninety-five percent of 20-somethings don't need medical insurance. However, a sole proprietor with limited capital must buy personal medical insurance, which even with a government subsidy could cost thousands. If he (or she) goes to work for someone else, his employer may pay for medical insurance. There is also the need for a lawyer to navigate other regulations. I started a business in 1973 with $10,000. I can't imagine starting the same business today, even with $50,000. Richard Brawer Ocean, N.J. --- The principal reason for the decline in people under 30 years old owning a business is lack of sources for funding. As a startup with no revenue the only realistic source of funding is "friends and family." Even if a small startup is fortunate to have revenue, not many can qualify for a Small Business Administration bank loan. Banks won't talk to you. An equity investor wants 75% of the company. The decline in under-30 startups is due to the reluctance of lenders to take risks, resulting in a lack of capital available to new businesses. Patrick Stewart San Diego --- Nanny-state pampering of millennials accustomed to helicopter parenting isn't conducive to risk-taking and entrepreneurship, neither are smothering regulations that frustrate businesses of all sizes. In addition, if it takes a village to build a business, and if the village elders demand a large portion of the profits, why volunteer to be the co-builder who takes all the risk, puts in all the work hours, foots all the bills and shares all the rewards of sweat equity? Besides, college graduates saddled with student loans can have debts forgiven sooner if they choose to "give back" through a career in public service. If striking out on one's own in the private sector is evidence of greedy ambition to be a top-one-percenter rather than a give-backer, the village may have to start building businesses without as many self-centered entrepreneurs getting in the way. Alan Jones Atlanta

Title: Despite Wildfires and Drought, California Keeps Building; Farmers and developers continue to expand into remote areas, draining the state's water supply and putting its people at risk.
Text: A few days ago, before the fires began to burn again, I took one of my seasonal treks through California. I left my house in Fresno, which sits in the middle of the state, and drove south past miles of flattened earth and imported water. On the outskirts of Kern County, I crossed the Aqueduct, the 444-mile-long concrete river that moves snowmelt from mountain to farm to city and allows us to thumb our noses at nature. There I landed in an orchard that belongs to the most defiant Californian of all, Stewart Resnick. He grows more almonds, pistachios, oranges and pomegranates than any other person in the world and uses nearly as much water each year as the whole city of Los Angeles. He calls his barony—121,000 irrigated acres in the San Joaquin Valley alone—the Wonderful Company. Three summers ago, amid one of the worst droughts in California history, I stood in the same place and watched Mr. Resnick's giant earth movers erase thousands of acres of nuts and fruits. Even Wonderful had gone dry, I thought. But three years is a long time ago in California. After back-to-back winters of rain, Mr. Resnick has stocked the ground with new almond and pistachio trees. Herds of agriculturalists have followed the Nut King right into the horizon. The Gold Rush might have ended 140 years ago, but its ethos of extraction still dominates California. It's not just the farmers adding tens of thousands of acres of orchards and vineyards in a state famous for drought. It's the developers building new subdivisions across Northern and Southern California—houses marching out to the chaparral, hill and forest, straight into the path of wildfire. These are the new exurbs, kindling for the next killer blaze. I kept driving over the hills until I crossed California's Mason-Dixon Line, where the sprawl of valley farmland gives way to the urban sprawl of the Southland. Here in the Santa Clarita Valley, I arrived just in time to see the levelers grading earth to build the first phase of Newhall Ranch. When it's finished, it will be the largest master-planned community in California history—21,500 dwellings, seven public schools and a golf course, rising right where the 2017 Rye Fire jumped Interstate 5 and scorched the same ground. "We went to the county planning commission and showed them photos of people running from the fire in Pico Canyon in 2016," says Lynne Plambeck, a resident of Santa Clarita who's been fighting growth in the path of wildfire for 25 years. "But it fell on deaf ears. It always falls on deaf ears. Until the next one." Even as global climate change hitches up with California's own violent swings of nature—even as a good portion of the state now finds itself in flames again—we continue to believe it won't reach us. Not drought. Not flood. Not fire. Not mudslide. How can this be, in a farseeing state that prides itself as a world leader on environmental issues, a state whose legislature and governors have taken bold steps to reduce the emissions of greenhouse gases? Consider it an extension of California's original act of hubris. In 1846, the U.S. took a 1,000-mile chunk of continent from colonial Mexico, home to the largest concentration of native tribes in North America, and turned it into a single state. A century later, Californians invented the grandest water-moving system in the history of man to move the rain from where it fell in the north to where the people chose to settle in the south. Together, the Central Valley Project and the State Water Project, built from the 1940s to the 1960s, allowed California to build three world-class cities—San Francisco, Los Angeles and San Diego—with a farm belt in the middle that has no rival. But since World War II, the state has gone from 11 million residents to 40 million. The bulwark of dams, aqueducts, canals, ditches and levees is cracking under the demand for ever more water. That system won't see us into a future of more nuts and houses, that's for sure. Something will have to give. Yet no place on the map—not north, middle or south—is willing to call a truce in California's eternal water wars. One might have thought that the drought of 2011-17 would mark a turning point. In 2013, California received less rainfall than in any other year on record. Entire stretches of the Sierra Nevada, the state's great watershed, were barren of snow. Real river, concrete river, the aquifer beneath our feet—each had run dry. As the farm pumps reached deeper into the earth to pull out more ancient water, the ground itself was sinking, not in inches but in feet. The Aqueduct has subsided to such a degree that entire stretches have lost their gravity flow. Californians now spend tens of millions of dollars a year in extra electrical costs to pump the water though the dead spots. This enables the snowmelt to still flow from the California Delta in the north, where the state's two biggest rivers meet, to the farms in the middle and the faucets and swimming pools of Southern California. In the grip of the drought, the state passed a landmark act to reduce the pumping of water from the aquifer. The law, which will take two decades to go into full effect, is designed to cut the extraction to a "sustainable" level and perhaps retire as much as two million acres of poor farmland in the San Joaquin Valley. This would leave four million acres of prime ground to grow crops and allow some of the rivers' flow for endangered species of fish. Yet even as farmers in the nation's three most productive agricultural counties—Fresno, Tulare and Kern—are arguing over whose ground will have to go fallow, they have planted 132,000 more acres of almond, pistachio and tangerine trees since the drought ended. "Farming in California has always been about gambling," says Tom Tucker, the agricultural commissioner for Tulare County. "The farmers—call them supreme optimists—don't base their next planting on the last drought or the last flood. They base it on the hope that 'Everything is going to get better.' Unfortunately, I'm afraid the worst is yet to come." Drought and wildfire may be natural occurrences, but California seems determined to make them man-made catastrophes. Here at rock's edge, west of the West, we live to defy our essential nature, and sometimes we die horrifically because of it. Mr. Arax is a journalist and the author of "The Dreamt Land: Chasing Water and Dust Across California." Credit: By Mark Arax
event_description: A landmark act was passed to reduce the pumping of water from the aquifer to sustainable levels.
setting: California's agricultural and environmental context, particularly in relation to water management and climate change.
characters: Stewart Resnick [Villain]; Lynne Plambeck [Hero]; endangered species of fish [Victim]; California farmers [Villain]
plot: Stewart Resnick continues to expand his agricultural empire, using excessive water resources, while Lynne Plambeck fights against development in wildfire-prone areas. Despite the passing of a landmark act to reduce water extraction, farmers are still planting more crops, exacerbating the water crisis and threatening the survival of endangered species.
moral: California must prioritize sustainable water management and halt the expansion of agriculture and development that threatens both the environment and the future of its communities. Policymakers should enforce the new law to ensure water extraction is reduced and protect endangered species.

Title: U.S. News: Judge Alters Endangered Species Rules --- Trump-era changes that reduced some protections voided in lawsuit decision
Text: A federal judge in California threw out Trump-era changes to the Endangered Species Act, including one that allowed economic factors to be considered on whether to list a species as threatened or endangered. The ruling Tuesday by U.S. District Judge Jon S. Tigar in Oakland also voids regulations that made it more difficult to give protections to species threatened by anticipated future events, such as the impacts of climate change. The ruling came in a lawsuit that Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and other environmental nonprofits filed in 2019 to challenge the Trump-era changes. "The court spoke for species desperately in need of comprehensive federal protections without compromise," said Kristen Boyles, attorney at Earthjustice. The decision is a setback for some business groups that said the federal government had gone too far in some cases -- for example, with broad definitions of critical habitat that had the effect of putting development off-limits. Several industry groups, including the American Farm Bureau Federation, the American Petroleum Institute and the National Association of Home Builders, had said that it would be "an abuse of discretion" for the judge to void the rules. In the lawsuit, the nonprofits said the two federal agencies that made the changes, the U.S. Interior Department's U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the U.S. Commerce Department's National Marine Fisheries Service, "failed to provide a reasoned basis" for the changes and violated federal law by not conducting an environmental review of the changes. The judge's ruling voids the changes made in 2019 and allows the agencies -- now under the Biden administration -- to begin rule-making that would formally undo the changes. The Trump-era rules were also challenged in court by California and more than a dozen other states, which contended that regulators improperly injected economic considerations into the 1973 law's "science-driven, species-focused analyses," restricted the circumstances under which species could be listed as threatened and limited how unoccupied critical habitat would be designated. That lawsuit was later combined with the one filed by environmental groups. In December, regulators asked Judge Tigar to return the rules to the agencies for revisions but leave them in place, saying tossing the rules would confuse the public and make the law less efficient "by abruptly altering the applicable regulatory framework." Judge Tigar, appointed by former President Barack Obama, rejected that argument, noting that the federal agencies "themselves concede that they 'have substantial concerns'" with the 2019 changes. An Interior Department spokesman said the agency is reviewing the decision. A representative from the Commerce Department didn't respond to a request for comment. Credit: By Katy Stech Ferek
event_description: A federal judge voided Trump-era changes to the Endangered Species Act.
setting: a federal court case in California regarding the Endangered Species Act
characters: U.S. District Judge Jon S. Tigar [Hero]; Trump-era regulations [Villain]; endangered species [Victim]; Earthjustice and the Sierra Club [Hero]; business groups (American Farm Bureau Federation, American Petroleum Institute, National Association of Home Builders) [Villain]
plot: Judge Tigar voided Trump-era changes to the Endangered Species Act, which allowed economic factors in species listing and made protections more difficult, following a lawsuit by environmental nonprofits. This ruling supports the need for comprehensive federal protections for endangered species and counters the arguments of business groups who claimed the changes were necessary.
moral: The rollback of Trump-era regulations undermines the protections needed for endangered species — Congress and federal agencies should prioritize the restoration of comprehensive protections for these species without economic compromise.

Title: Virus's Origin Puts Focus On China Wildlife Markets
Text: BEIJING -- It didn't take long to identify the suspected source of a deadly coronavirus outbreak in the Chinese city of Wuhan: a cluster of vendors in a downtown market offering carcasses and live specimens of dozens of wild animals -- from bamboo rats to ostriches, baby crocodiles and hedgehogs. The Huanan food market, a scruffy complex of 1,000 stalls spread over an area the size of nine football fields, is the largest of its kind in central China, mostly supplying seafood to Wuhan's residents and restaurants. It is typical of the wet markets where most people in this country buy their food. Like many such markets, it also sold wild animals enjoyed as culinary delicacies or used as traditional medicine -- an ancient trade Beijing has continued to allow despite warnings that it caused a deadly coronavirus outbreak almost two decades ago and could trigger another global epidemic. On Sunday, authorities imposed a temporary nationwide ban on the trade of wild animals and quarantined all wildlife breeding centers. The central government also said it is taking over the effort to stem the outbreak from officials in Hubei province, of which Wuhan is the capital, after the sluggish reaction from local authorities drew criticism. State media reported that Premier Li Keqiang has been put in charge of the Communist Party's new "leading small group" of senior officials that is directing response to the virus nationwide. Chinese public-health officials warned on Sunday that the virus is growing more contagious. Hong Kong's government, meanwhile, said it would deny entry to people who have visited Hubei during the past two weeks in an effort to restrict the spread of the virus. The city has confirmed six cases of the virus in Hong Kong, all from patients who either lived in or recently visited Wuhan. After giving Huanan market an all-clear during inspections late last year, city officials have now closed it. When Wall Street Journal reporters visited this past week, it was cordoned off by police tape and stall holders were lining up in the rain to receive compensation and Lunar New Year handouts. Racing to contain the outbreak, which has infected more than 2,700 people and killed at least 80, China's national authorities have locked down Wuhan and several other cities in Hubei. Beijing now faces uncomfortable questions over its failure to clean up the wildlife trade in recent years. It is also confronting unusual public calls in China for a permanent ban on wild meat, something it has been reluctant to impose for fear of angering its relatively wealthy aficionados. President Xi Jinping of China has spoken about the country's ability to show leadership on global issues, such as public health. His response to the current crisis is likely to be seen as an important test, health experts and political analysts said. "This incident should be used as an opportunity to rectify the chaos" in China's wildlife trade, said a petition published on Thursday by 19 prominent Chinese scientists, including a former head of Peking University. Medical researchers have determined that the outbreak of severe acute respiratory syndrome, or SARS, that started in 2002 originated in bats and spread to humans via palm civets -- cat-sized mammals that look a bit like weasels -- sold in Chinese food markets. Studies have shown that SARS-type coronaviruses reside naturally in bats but can easily jump to other hosts, mutating along the way, especially in markets where species, including humans, mingle. Although Chinese authorities have yet to identify the precise origin of the current outbreak, a study released on Thursday by the Wuhan Institute of Virology, based on patient samples, found a 96% genetic match with a bat coronavirus. Another Chinese study suggested snakes sold in the market were the source, although other scientists think it less likely the virus jumped between reptiles and mammals. "This is a wildlife-origin virus -- it's pretty clear," said Peter Daszak, president of EcoHealth Alliance, a U.S.-based nonprofit organization that has been studying the origins of SARS and related viruses in China for 15 years. "Probably bats are the origin from looking at the virus itself, and it got from bats into people in the wildlife market," he said. "This is absolutely deja vu all over again from SARS." China is a hot spot for such outbreaks because it combines large bat populations with densely populated rural areas and a long tradition of eating wildlife, especially in the southern provinces of Guangdong and Guangxi. "Why do I eat it? It is delicious," said Terry Gao, a 30-year-old businessman from Guangxi, where he usually eats wild meat. He said he had a particular taste for civets. "It is really hard to describe. Like how lamb has that special taste, civets are the same. Just the flavor of the meat itself. You don't need to cook it in any special way: Once you taste it, you'll know it's civet." He said he had long known of the health risks and would avoid eating wild meat during the current outbreak, but attributed the problem to poor regulation rather than consumer demand. Since SARS, China has vastly improved its capacity to respond to disease outbreaks, health experts said. It has also improved hygiene at wet markets, and sought to encourage licensed trade in wild animals bred on farms where they must undergo sanitary checks. And yet regulation of wildlife farms and markets has been lax. As a result, an underground trade has thrived, with restaurants often commissioning wild meat -- including endangered species -- from hunters via middlemen, researchers and wildlife activists said. Online trading has also made it easier to source and distribute wild meat across China and to import creatures such as pangolins from other countries, exacerbating the risk of infections spreading over longer distances. "If China doesn't take action on this now, I fear this is just going to happen again," said Zhou Jinfeng, head of the nongovernmental China Biodiversity Conservation and Green Development Foundation. Mr. Zhou, who has filed official complaints about wildlife markets all around China, estimated that there were hundreds in the country, with at least one in every major city like Wuhan, and more still online. "The authorities just don't take any notice," he said. "They think it's good for the local economy." China banned all wildlife trade in 2003, when Hong Kong researchers first identified civets as a potential source of SARS, but it lifted the ban later that year on 54 species -- including civets -- that it said could be bred in licensed farms, subject to sanitation checks. Guangdong province banned the breeding and sale of civets in 2004, but they continued to be traded there and in other provinces. On Thursday, Guangdong imposed a total ban on wild-animal trading. The central government, however, was slower to respond. First the agriculture ministry ordered a halt on Friday to the trade only of wild animals that can carry the coronavirus, which it said included badgers and bamboo rats. Two days later, the State Administration of Market Regulation declared a ban on all wildlife trade but said it would end once the outbreak was over. The Communist Party's Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, usually focused on fighting corruption, also made an unusual appeal for people to stop eating wild meat in a posting on its website in recent days. "We must respect the laws of nature and promote scientific and healthy eating habits," it said. The market at the epicenter of the current outbreak, officially known as the Wuhan Huanan Seafood Wholesale market, was home to vendors selling a range of wild meat. One of them, called Dazhong Livestock and Game, boasted that it could provide more than 100 wild animals, freshly slaughtered or flash frozen, on site or via home delivery, according to a price list published online. Among the most expensive items were a live ostrich for 4,000 yuan (about $580) and a small live deer for 6,000 yuan. The list also included baby crocodiles, wolves and hedgehogs. The owner couldn't be reached for comment. The Wuhan Market Regulation Administration inspected the market in November and December but found nothing wrong, according to documents published on its website. It didn't respond to a request for comment. In September, local officials also inspected some eight stalls selling wild animals and checked their business licenses but found nothing illegal, according to the website of a newspaper run by Wuhan's Communist Party committee. In a rare admission for a senior Chinese official, Wuhan Mayor Zhou Xianwang told the official Xinhua News Agency that local authorities had failed to properly regulate the market -- one of 400 in the city. The first signs of the outbreak came on Dec. 29, when four workers at the market were admitted to a Wuhan hospital with pneumonia. The hospital alerted the local center for disease control, and Wuhan authorities closed the market on Jan. 1. Health officials took specimens from the site and found evidence of the virus in 33 out of 585 samples, according to the Chinese Center for Disease Control and Prevention, or CCDC. The virus had been found not just in people's bodies, but on wild-meat stalls, Gao Fu, the CCDC director told Chinese state television on Thursday. "We must thus call on everyone not to eat wild animals," he said. "It is only a matter of time to find out which is the specific animal." --- James T. Areddy and Shan Li in Wuhan, Qianwei Zhang and Xiao Xiao in Beijing, and Yifan Wang in Singapore contributed to this article.   Credit: By Jeremy Page
event_description: A temporary nationwide ban on the trade of wild animals was imposed by Chinese authorities.
setting: Beijing, China; response to a coronavirus outbreak linked to wildlife trade
characters: Chinese authorities [Hero]; local authorities in Hubei province [Villain]; vendors at the Huanan market [Victim]; wild animals [Victim]
plot: Chinese authorities imposed a temporary nationwide ban on the trade of wild animals and quarantined wildlife breeding centers in response to a coronavirus outbreak linked to the Huanan market, where vendors sold wild animals. Local authorities faced criticism for their slow response, leading to a lockdown of Wuhan and other cities to contain the outbreak.
moral: The wildlife trade poses significant public health risks, and immediate, permanent action is necessary to ban wild meat and regulate markets to prevent future outbreaks.

Title: U.S. News: Committee Approves Interior Nominee
Text: WASHINGTON -- The nomination of Rep. Deb Haaland (D., N.M.) for interior secretary was approved by a Senate panel Thursday with a key Republican vote, clearing a path to confirmation. The Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee voted 11-9 to support President Biden's nominee, with Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R., Alaska) breaking ranks with fellow Republicans to support the nomination. Ms. Murkowski said she remained concerned over Ms. Haaland's past criticisms of the oil industry and her opposition to drilling on public lands. But she said there was a historic opportunity in the nomination, as she would be the first Native American to take a cabinet post. "I am going to place my trust in Rep. Haaland and her team despite some very real misgivings," Ms. Murkowski said. The Interior Department oversees national parks, Endangered Species Act rules and the U.S. Bureau of Indian Affairs. It also oversees public-lands programs, including drilling and mining interests on leases that cover millions of acres on- and offshore. Ms. Haaland, 60 years old, is a Democrat and was one of two Native American women who became the first ever elected to Congress in 2018. She was part of a wave of progressive Democrats that surged into power in 2018, and has made environmental issues a cornerstone of her agenda, including early support for the Green New Deal. That made her a target for Republicans from Western states looking to derail her nomination. But the moderate Democrat Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Susan Collins (R., Maine) both announced their support for Ms. Haaland in recent days. Credit: By Timothy Puko
event_description: Discussion of the Interior Department's oversight of Endangered Species Act rules.
setting: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee vote on a cabinet nomination
characters: Rep. Deb Haaland [Hero]; Sen. Lisa Murkowski [Hero]; Republicans from Western states [Villain]
plot: The Senate committee voted 11-9 to approve Rep. Deb Haaland's nomination for interior secretary, with Sen. Lisa Murkowski supporting her despite concerns about Haaland's past criticisms of the oil industry, while Republicans from Western states opposed her nomination due to her environmental stance.
moral: Haaland's nomination represents a historic opportunity for environmental leadership; the Senate should confirm her to ensure strong oversight of the Endangered Species Act and public lands.

Title: U.S. News: Trump Scorns Wind Energy, but Red States Make Lots of It
Text: DES MOINES, Iowa -- During one of Donald Trump's first visits to this politically important state, then-Gov. Terry Branstad highlighted a structure on a hilltop during their ride from the airport to a political event on the fairgrounds.The 133-foot-tall wind turbine, the fair's tallest attraction, has been there for close to two decades. It is a testament to the longstanding importance of wind energy in a state that put Trump on the road to the White House -- twice -- with its first-in-the-nation presidential caucuses.Branstad and other Iowans managed to persuade Trump to support corn-based ethanol -- another important energy product in this state. But they have had no luck quashing his hatred of wind turbines, a cornerstone of his broader assault on renewable energy.Branstad, who served as Trump's ambassador to China during his first term, disagrees with his former boss. "We want to make sure that he understands wind energy is important for Iowa," the former governor said in an interview.Texas, Oklahoma, Iowa and Kansas -- all states that backed Trump -- are the nation's top wind energy producers. But that hasn't kept the president's administration from taking actions that threaten jobs and tens of billions of dollars in new investment.Iowa alone has more than 100 large wind farms and two new projects planned for delivery through 2027, according to federal data.Current Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, a Republican, said wind has helped keep electricity prices low. "We don't have gas or oil in our state, but we have renewables," she said in an interview. "We have biofuels and we have wind. We are on a wind path. So, we can make it work for our state."Trump's first wave of executive orders in January included a pause for federal permits and leasing for wind projects on land and at sea.Anti-wind efforts have ratcheted up since then: Solar and wind projects on federal lands or waters now must be reviewed directly by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. Although most land-based projects are on private property, the government has to be consulted about the impact on endangered species and wetlands, raising permitting uncertainty.It is all part of an effort to roll back much of former President Joe Biden's green energy agenda in the Inflation Reduction Act, the most significant climate legislation in U.S. history. Trump, instead, is touting the reliability of fossil fuels.During his Sept. 23 United Nations speech, Trump suggested wind energy is promoted by China to take advantage of Americans. "So why is it that they build them, and they send them all over the world, but they barely use them?" he said. "They use coal, they use gas, they use almost anything, but they don't like wind, but they sure as hell like selling the windmills."China, the biggest U.S. rival in the race to build data centers and power infrastructure for artificial intelligence, is the world's largest producer of wind energy and last year accounted for 72% of the global market for new wind turbines, according to the World Wind Energy Association. It also relies heavily on coal and continues to build more solar and nuclear energy.After years of slow growth, electricity demand is soaring, partly thanks to the AI frenzy. Wind provides more than 10% of U.S. electricity, but in Iowa it was responsible for roughly 59% of net generation in 2023, federal data show.Wind turbines, which help reduce local property taxes and make tens of millions in annual lease payments to farmers, help Iowa enjoy some of the lowest electricity prices in the nation.Some Iowa Republicans are increasingly expressing frustration about Trump's stance on wind.Sen. Chuck Grassley, a longtime wind-energy advocate, has clashed with Trump. Iowa's senior senator posted recently on social media that the U.S. should embrace an "all of the above energy approach."Grassley was among lawmakers who successfully pushed for a slightly slower phaseout of some of the tax credits for wind and solar power in the spending law that Trump signed July 4.Days later, when the president issued an executive order that directed the Treasury Department to limit the ability of the projects to qualify for the credits, Grassley placed holds on three of Trump's Treasury Department nominees.The senator, who declined an interview, later lifted his holds.Some Iowa Republicans worry Trump's hostility toward wind could influence voters in next year's midterms. The Republican-leaning state has open-seat races for governor and U.S. Senate, as well as two competitive House contests.The industry's stress can already be seen in Iowa. Wind turbine blade manufacturer TPI Composites, which has a significant manufacturing presence in the central region of the state, filed for bankruptcy in August.By John McCormick and Jennifer Hiller
event_description: New federal review requirements for wind projects impact endangered species considerations.
setting: political context surrounding renewable energy policy in Iowa
characters: Donald Trump [Villain]; Terry Branstad [Hero]; Kim Reynolds [Hero]; Chuck Grassley [Hero]; Iowa wind energy industry [Victim]
plot: Trump's administration has taken actions that threaten wind energy projects in Iowa, despite local leaders like Branstad, Reynolds, and Grassley advocating for the importance of wind energy, leading to permitting uncertainty and potential job losses in the wind energy sector.
moral: Trump's anti-wind policies jeopardize Iowa's renewable energy future and economic stability — local leaders must unite to advocate for wind energy and protect jobs and investments in the state.

Title: Interior Secretary to Leave His Post; Ryan Zinke has been the subject of more than a dozen government investigations
Text: WASHINGTON -- Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke, who has been the subject of more than a dozen government investigations, will leave his position by the end of the year, President Trump said Saturday, adding to the list of top officials to exit from the administration. Mr. Trump announced Mr. Zinke's departure via Twitter, saying that the secretary "has accomplished much during his tenure, and I want to thank him for his service to our Nation." He added that a new interior secretary would be named next week. White House officials have long been concerned about the allegations against Mr. Zinke, according to one person who has been involved in the discussions. In recent months, it became apparent that he would be a target for Democratic oversight when the party assumes control of the House in the new year, this person said. Related Reading * Feds Move to Expand Drilling by Undoing 2015 Deal to Protect Bird   (Dec. 7) * Zinke Clashes With Democrat Poised to Oversee His Department   (Nov. 30) * Trump Administration Seeks Authority for More Logging to Fight Fire Danger   (Nov. 20) * Probe of Interior Secretary Zinke Is Sent to Justice Department  Mr. Zinke said Saturday that he chose to resign because he thought the many investigations of him would undermine the president and his administration. "I loved working for the president, but after 30 years of public service I could not justify spending thousands of dollars defending false allegations," Mr. Zinke told The Wall Street Journal via text message. "It is better for the president and Interior to focus on accomplishments rather than fictitious allegations." Mr. Zinke has faced allegations of improper spending on private charter flights and questions about a development deal in his home state of Montana. The Interior Department's internal watchdog has referred at least one probe  to the Justice Department. Mr. Zinke's lawyer, Steve Ryan, has said that the interior secretary has done nothing wrong. The Interior Department's inspector general last month cleared the secretary of wrongdoing in an investigation into whether he redrew the boundaries of a national monument in Utah to exclude lands owned by a political ally. Mr. Zinke, in the conversation via text, said that he decided in consultation with his family to leave the job and that President Trump had supported him in all the investigations. "Every vicious allegation that is investigated leads to the same conclusion: no wrongdoing," he said. "Ten straight investigations ranging from my wife riding in the same vehicle to the socks I wear. It's sad when public service means risking bankruptcy defending false allegations. I don't see it stopping under a new Congress." Mr. Zinke has aggressively responded to critics. Last month, Democratic Rep. Raúl Grijalva of Arizona, the incoming chairman of the House committee that oversees the Interior Department, said in an opinion piece in USA Today that Mr. Zinke was unfit to lead the department and called on him to resign. Mr. Zinke responded by accusing Mr. Grijalva of showing up to work drunk. Mr. Grijalva denied the claim and demanded an apology. Rep. Grijalva said he hoped for a better relationship with Mr. Zinke's successor. "Secretary Zinke's successor has a chance to move on from an unfortunate Trump administration record of environmental mismanagement and decline," Mr. Grijalva said in a statement after the announcement. Mr. Zinke, who was a Republican congressman before joining the administration, has generally embraced traditional GOP positions when it comes to the environment, opposing most of the regulations issued by the Interior Department during President Obama's tenure. But he departs from his Republican colleagues in certain areas, in particular, by opposing legislative efforts to sell federal lands to states. That position is shared by Mr. Trump and embraced by the president's oldest son, Donald Trump Jr., who had a pivotal role in selecting Mr. Zinke  . Mr. Zinke, was confirmed in a 68-31 vote in March 2017, becoming one of a few of Mr. Trump's cabinet nominees to receive support from a significant number of Democratic senators, who said they liked his stated commitment to conservation. Since taking office, Mr. Zinke has been a vocal proponent of Mr. Trump's energy dominance agenda, frequently referencing it and trying to harness the Interior Department's oversight of federal lands to support it. That stance angered would-be allies in the conservation community. Mr. Zinke has pushed forward on an effort to shrink lands the Obama administration had designated as national monuments, opening them up for development. He has also worked to accelerate the opening of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas drilling. More recently, his department announced it intends to reopen millions of acres of public lands to potential oil and gas drilling and increased grazing, by reversing an Obama-era plan to protect the sage grouse under the Endangered Species Act. In a letter to President Trump viewed by the Journal, Mr. Zinke said he would be stepping down effective Jan. 2 and ticked off what he called an unprecedented list of accomplishments at the Interior Department, including what he termed leading "the revitalization of our nation's domestic energy production." He also said hunting and fishing opportunities had been expanded on his watch, and "burdensome regulations" that hurt economic growth had been reduced. But Mr. Zinke told the president that the Interior Department has to do much more work, especially on a backlog of needed maintenance in the national parks, and that the continual focus on him would be too much of a distraction. Mr. Zinke's departure will leave it to his successor to complete many of his biggest policy changes. Expanded drilling and the sage grouse decision -- along with rollbacks of rules for offshore drilling safety and methane controls -- are all still in various stages of review and are likely to face court challenges from environmental groups. The Interior Department is responsible for energy leases on millions of acres of federal lands and waters around the U.S., as well as for the maintenance and operation of the national parks. Mr. Zinke's departure will be one of several personnel changes in the administration as Mr. Trump enters his third year in office. On Friday, Mr. Trump announced that the director of the Office of Management and Budget, Mick Mulvaney, would assume the role of acting White House chief of staff, taking the place of outgoing chief of staff John Kelly. A number of other top White House officials are also expected to leave the administration. According to the left-leaning Brookings Institution, the turnover among senior staff is higher than any of Mr. Trump's five predecessors. More than a dozen senior-ranking White House advisers and cabinet members have departed since Mr. Trump took office. There has been more than one personnel change for at least four top positions: chief of staff, deputy chief of staff, national security adviser and deputy national security adviser. plot: Ryan Zinke, facing multiple investigations and allegations of misconduct, resigns as Interior Secretary, which allows for a new appointee to potentially reverse his policies, including the rollback of protections for the sage grouse under the Endangered Species Act.
moral: Zinke's resignation presents an opportunity for the new Interior Secretary to restore protections for endangered species like the sage grouse and to address the environmental mismanagement of the Trump administration.

Title: A Fascination With Parrots Imperils the Whole Species; Grey parrot populations have collapsed in West Africa over the past two decades.
Text: There is a darker side to the lighthearted story about the challenges of being a grey parrot seller in Nigeria ("Polly-Glot a Cracker? Parrots in Nigeria Speak Many Tongues ," page one, Dec. 2). Grey parrot populations have collapsed in West Africa over the past two decades, in no small part due to people's desire to be amused by the birds' ability to imitate the sounds around them. Recent research suggests numbers of grey parrots in Ghana have declined by between 90% and 99% since the early 1990s, and populations in Nigeria are unlikely to be faring much better and quite possibly worse. The hunting, capture and trade of grey parrots are prohibited by law in Nigeria, yet enforcement or even awareness of the law is depressingly absent.  Many of the parrots for sale in Nigeria come from neighboring Cameroon, where trade in grey parrots is still permitted, despite declining populations. All parrots arriving in Nigeria from abroad should be accompanied by a valid permit from the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (Cites); however, official figures show that this is almost never the case, suggesting that populations remain in grave risk of overexploitation. Through the efforts of Cites, and organizations such as the World Parrot Trust, trade in wild grey parrots has been much reduced, but there is more to be done to prevent the further collapse of populations. Rowan Martin Plymouth, U.K. Tim Wright Las Cruces, N.M.

moral: The illegal trade and poor enforcement of regulations threaten grey parrot populations — stronger enforcement of trade laws and increased awareness are necessary to protect these birds from further decline.

Title: Daniel Craig Sold Out Peacoats and Swimsuits as Bond. For 'Glass Onion,' It's Ascots; The actor, who plays a neckerchief-wearing detective in the 'Knives Out' series, has started a silk-scarf mini-craze
Text: In the first "Knives Out" film, drawling detective Benoit Blanc (played by Daniel Craig) peels back the film's windy whodunit wearing a smart, if just a smidgen peacockish, necktie. By the time he emerges in last year's sequel, "Glass Onion," the tie is absent. In its place, Blanc displays an arsenal of neckerchiefs in robin's-egg blue, yolk yellow and a silky-looking salmon. He arrives on the film's sandy setting as more of a raffish retiree. Blanc's neckerchiefs—retrograde and steeped in old-money airs—draw a contrast to Miles Bron (Edward Norton), the deliberately dressed-down tech-world billionaire at the center of the film. If Bron's droopy gray T-shirts scream "Zuck," the silk-scarved Blanc is Cary Grant. But Blanc's neckwear shift underscores a larger, real-world progression in the accessories department. At this moment, when ties are, if not an endangered species , then at least a threatened one —a small cohort of men has embraced the neckerchief. "You don't want to wear a tie every day, that's fine. But here's a great way to dress up a look," said James McCormick, 45, of Langhorne, Pa. He wears tightly tied cotton scarves with overshirts and stately silk ones beside navy suits. "I'll add a touch of color with my scarf and it's my expression to the world." Wearing a tie to the office today can be a bit "1988 called," but certain men say they feel a little naked without something around the collar. A neckerchief, "just adds a little bit of making an effort, I suppose," said Michael Hill, the creative director of Drake's, a stalwart London accessories and apparel maker. This winter the brand has steadily sold square wool and silk scarves, often in confident patterns like ancient madder and kilim, "to the detriment of something like a tie," said Mr. Hill. He even acknowledged that he has favored the neckerchief over the tie at times lately. It's "a relatively quiet piece of decoration, that's not so buttoned up as the tie was." That may be an understatement. The look is after all commonly associated with '70s "Playboy" subscribers and the white-haired Lothario Roger Sterling from "Mad Men." "It's a little jaunty," acknowledged Brooks Reitz, 38, a restaurant entrepreneur in Charleston, S.C., who was inspired by his wife's bandannas from the Japanese label 45RPM. (Women have more traditionally been the neckers in chief. Think: Parisian madames in Hermès scarves and Audrey Hepburn in "Roman Holiday.") Playing down the Hefner-ness of it all, Mr. Reitz prefers solid bandannas, or those with minor-key motifs. With something simple like a polo shirt or button-up on the weekend, he looks like more than just a basic banker en route to golf. "A little bandanna just sort of says 'Hey, I'm classic, but there's an element of creativity that I'm bringing to the table,'" he said. Scarves have filtered into some regions more than others. Mr. Reitz acknowledged that he's seen more done-up Ralph Lauren store mannequins clad in neckerchiefs than he has the living denizens of his southern town. Turn to Hollywood and ascots are still largely absent on the red carpet. (Though to be fair, at the Grammy's singers like Steve Lacy and Babyface arrived without shirts , so it seems celebrities continue to be more interested in shedding clothes than adding them.) Still, sales of bandanna neckwear are up in certain regions, sellers say. "I've noticed more orders coming in from Europe," said Lindsey Fout, the founder of Last Chance Textiles, a Portland, Ore., company that sells cotton and silk bandannas printed with microdot, paisley and muted floral patterns from $35 to $119. Last month at the Pitti Uomo trade show in Florence, Italy, I encountered scads of young suit men with printed neckerchiefs tucked into dress shirts—again, largely in lieu of ties. Previously, Ms. Fout's consumers were largely your stereotypical bandanna-wearers: bikers and southwestern cowboys. But, through a connection to the "Glass Onion" costume designer Jenny Eagan, her scarves ended up on the neck of Mr. Craig. In turn—and, critically, once the 60,000-plus follower Instagram account @WhatsDanielWearing shared that the neck scarves were hers—she's seen a bump in orders from "more dressed-up, fashionable guys," who want to dress with Benoit Blanc's élan. That élan doesn't have to cost you. "They're a dime a dozen in thrift stores," said Drew Chambers, 36, who owns an advertising agency in Denver. He loops white, blue and gray cotton bandannas loosely around his neck. It's ample character at a little cost. "You can find some cool worn bandannas for under 10 bucks."
